title: Friction: how hard is the grip, and what decides it?

summary.text: Load a box with more weight and it needs a harder pull to move. Turn the same box onto its narrow side, so less of it touches the floor, and the pull barely changes. Friction grows with how hard two things press together, not with how much of them you can see. That is because two surfaces really touch only at tiny spots, and pressing harder makes more spots touch. Three turns of thread round a pencil can hold a bottle of water, because each turn makes the grip several times stronger. Scientists still cannot work out friction from atoms alone.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a box on a floor with a magnifying glass showing two rough surfaces touching at only a few peaks, on the right a thread wound three times round a pencil holding up a water bottle.

intro.hook: Try this. Lay your hand flat on a table and press down gently. Slide your hand along. Now press down hard and slide again. When was it harder to slide, and why do you think so?
intro.text: At a harbour, one person can stop a huge boat with a rope and an iron post. No arm is that strong. In this unit you will find out what the rope is using. First you will test a simpler question. If you put more weight in a box, how much harder is it to pull? And does it matter which side of the box faces the floor? The answers surprise most people, and they explain the rope too.
intro.art: A hand pressing flat on a wooden table, with small arrows pointing down for the press and sideways for the slide, and a faint iron post with a rope wound round it in the background.

outcomes: I can say that friction grows when two surfaces press together harder, and that it also depends on what the two surfaces are made of.
I can run a fair test with a rubber band gauge, repeat each measurement, and show the results in a table and a graph.
I can explain why friction on a hard, flat surface hardly changes with the size of the face, using the idea of tiny real contact spots.
I can tell starting friction from sliding friction, and explain why things can stick and slip in jerks.
I can explain how rollers, wheels, ball bearings and oil lower friction, and why thick liquids drag.
I can explain how turns of a rope round a post make the grip several times stronger with every turn.
I can say that the work done against friction turns into heat, and work it out as friction force times distance.
I can say what scientists agree about friction, and what they still do not know.

terms.meaning: The grip between two surfaces that touch. It works against sliding.
terms.example: A chappal does not slip on a dry road because of friction.
terms.art: A chappal pressed on a road, with a short arrow pointing backwards along the road.

terms.meaning: How hard two surfaces are pushed together. Scientists also call it the normal force.
terms.example: A box with a heavy load presses on the floor harder than an empty box.
terms.art: A box with sacks on it, and a big arrow pointing down into the floor.

terms.meaning: A number that says how grippy two surfaces are together. It is the friction force divided by the pressing force. It has no unit.
terms.example: Rubber on a dry road is about 0.8. Steel on ice is about 0.03.
terms.art: Two blocks on a ramp, one with a high number tag and one with a low number tag.

terms.meaning: Two things are proportional when one doubles whenever the other doubles.
terms.example: If a box with 1 kilogram needs 3 newtons of pull, a box with 2 kilograms needs about 6 newtons.
terms.art: A straight line on a graph starting at zero and climbing steadily.

terms.meaning: A tiny peak on a surface. Every surface has bumps, even one that feels smooth.
terms.example: Under a microscope, a polished steel spoon looks like a mountain range.
terms.art: A magnified surface drawn as a mountain range with peaks and valleys.

terms.meaning: The area of a surface that you can see and measure with a ruler.
terms.example: The big face of a shoebox has a larger apparent area than its end.
terms.art: A shoebox with its large face shaded in one colour and its narrow end in another.

terms.meaning: The tiny total area where two surfaces really touch, at the tips of their bumps. It is much smaller than the apparent area.
terms.example: A steel box on a steel table touches at only a tiny fraction of the face you see.
terms.art: Two mountain-range surfaces touching at three small peaks, with the touching spots coloured red.

terms.meaning: The friction that holds a thing still until you push hard enough to start it moving. Scientists call it static friction.
terms.example: A heavy almirah stays still until you push hard, and then it moves.
terms.art: A person pushing a cupboard that has not moved yet, with arrows of equal length.

terms.meaning: Motion in jerks. A thing sticks, then slips, then sticks again, over and over.
terms.example: A squeaking chalk, a squeaking door hinge and a violin bow all move by stick-slip.
terms.art: A chalk drawing a dotted line on a blackboard in small jerks.

terms.meaning: The friction on a wheel or ball that rolls without sliding. It is usually much smaller than sliding friction.
terms.example: A suitcase on wheels is much easier to pull than one dragged on the floor.
terms.art: A wheeled suitcase and a dragged suitcase side by side, with a short arrow and a long arrow.

terms.meaning: A ring of small balls that lets two parts turn past each other by rolling instead of sliding.
terms.example: A cycle wheel hub and a ceiling fan both have ball bearings.
terms.art: A metal ring of tiny balls between two rings, shown as a cut-open picture.

terms.meaning: How thick and slow a liquid is, because of the friction between its own parts. Honey has high viscosity and water has low viscosity.
terms.example: Honey pours slowly and water pours fast.
terms.art: A spoon of honey and a spoon of water pouring side by side, one in a thick slow stream.

terms.meaning: A short, strong post on a quay or pier that a rope is wound round to hold a boat.
terms.example: At Fort Kochi, boats are tied to iron bollards on the quay.
terms.art: An iron post on a stone quay with a rope wound three times round it.

terms.meaning: The sticking of two different things together by the pull between their atoms.
terms.example: A sticker sticks to a wall by adhesion.
terms.art: A sticker stuck to a tile with tiny arrows between its atoms and the tile's atoms.

explanations.concept: What decides how big friction is
explanations.definition: On a flat surface, the friction force is about equal to mu times the pressing force, where mu depends on the two surfaces.
explanations.description: On a flat floor, friction depends on two things. The first is how hard the two surfaces press together. The second is what the two surfaces are made of. Double the pressing force and the friction roughly doubles. Scientists write this as friction = mu times the pressing force. Mu is the coefficient of friction, a number that belongs to a pair of surfaces. A larger mu means a stronger grip. The rule is a good guide for hard, dry things, but it is not exact.
examples: A box with 2 kilograms in it needs about twice the pull of the same box with 1 kilogram in it.
Rubber on a dry road has a mu of about 0.8. Steel on ice has a mu of about 0.03, which is about 27 times less grip.
Pressing a finger hard on a pencil makes it harder to pull the pencil away.
explanations.art: A box on a floor with three loads stacked in turn and three arrows of growing length for the pull needed.
explanations.context: This card explains the first big result of the Press Harder test: how the pull changes when the load changes.

explanations.concept: Why a wide face and a narrow face grip about the same
explanations.definition: For hard, dry surfaces, friction is almost the same whatever the size of the face that touches. This is called Amontons's second law.
explanations.description: This rule surprises almost everyone. Take a box and lay it on its big face. Then stand it on its narrow side. The weight is the same, and the pull needed to start it is about the same. Many people expect the bigger face to grip more, because more of the box touches the floor. But the weight is the same, and the weight is what presses. A wider face spreads the same weight over more bumps, and each bump is pressed less. A narrower face puts the same weight on fewer bumps, and each bump is pressed more. The total grip comes out about equal. The rule works for hard, dry surfaces. It fails for soft things such as rubber, and for things that stick, like tape.
examples: A brick pulled on its big face or on its narrow end needs about the same pull.
A wide bicycle tyre and a thin one of the same bicycle brake in nearly the same distance on a dry, clean road. Racing tyres are special, because the rubber is soft and sticky.
A tractor on a muddy field needs wide, patterned wheels for a different reason. Mud is soft, and the wide wheel stops the wheel sinking.
explanations.art: A box lying flat and a box standing on its end, each with the same pull arrow, and a note that says the same weight.
explanations.context: This card explains the second result of the Press Harder test: why turning the box onto its side changes little.

explanations.concept: Why surfaces touch only at tiny spots
explanations.definition: Real contact area is the small total area where the bumps of two surfaces touch. It grows when the surfaces press together harder.
explanations.description: Under a microscope, even a polished surface is a mountain range. When you put two surfaces together, the peaks of one rest on the peaks of the other. They do not lie flat on each other like two sheets of paper. The area where they truly touch, called the real contact area, is a tiny fraction of the area you can see. For hard metals it is often less than one thousandth. Now press harder. The peaks that touch are squashed a little, and more peaks come into contact. Double the press and about double the real contact area. Friction comes from the grip at the touching spots. So doubling the pressing force doubles the real contact, and doubles the grip.
examples: Two steel plates pressed together carry electricity only through a few tiny spots, so the current is smaller than a full contact would allow.
Pressing your thumb harder on a table makes more of your skin touch the table.
Two sheets of paper on a desk touch at the high points of the paper fibres, with gaps everywhere else.
explanations.art: Two magnified rough surfaces touching at a few peaks, and a second picture where they are pressed harder and more peaks touch.
explanations.context: This card explains why the rules in the Press Harder test come out the way they do.

explanations.concept: Where does the grip really come from?
explanations.description: Everyone agrees that friction depends on the load and the materials. They do not fully agree on what happens at the touching spots. Three ideas have been put forward over three hundred years, and each seems to be partly right.
examples: Sandpaper clearly grips by catching on bumps.
Two clean, very smooth metal plates in a vacuum can weld themselves together, which bumps alone cannot explain.
A gecko walks up glass without any bumps for catching.

perspectives.who: Guillaume Amontons, a French scientist, in 1699, and many after him
perspectives.explanation: Surfaces grip because their bumps catch on each other. To slide, one surface must lift up and over the bumps of the other.

perspectives.who: Frank Bowden and David Tabor, at the University of Cambridge, in the 1940s and 1950s
perspectives.explanation: At the touching spots, the surfaces stick to each other, almost as if they were welded. Sliding means tearing these tiny joins apart again and again. Friction is the force needed to break them.

perspectives.who: Jacqueline Krim, a physicist in the United States, and other scientists who study friction between single layers of atoms, from the 1980s
perspectives.explanation: At the level of atoms, friction depends on how the atoms of the two surfaces line up, how they shake and how much heat they carry away. The old rules do not always hold at this tiny size.
All three ideas matter. Which one matters most depends on the materials and on the size we look at. No single theory yet predicts the friction of any pair of materials from atoms upward.

explanations.art: Three small drawings of two surfaces: bumps catching on bumps, atoms of two surfaces holding on to each other, and a thin layer of molecules between them.
explanations.context: This card is about the question that remains after the Press Harder test: what happens at the touching spots? Scientists still discuss it.

explanations.concept: Starting friction, sliding friction and stick-slip
explanations.definition: Starting friction holds a thing still up to a limit. Sliding friction is usually a little smaller. Stick-slip is the jerky movement that results.
explanations.description: Push a heavy box gently. It does not move, because friction pushes back just as hard as you push. Push a little harder and friction pushes back harder too. This goes on up to a limit. Past the limit, the box starts to move. The friction of a moving box is usually a little smaller than the limit. So the box jumps forward a little when it starts. Now imagine a thing being pulled slowly by a spring. It sticks, the spring stretches, the pull passes the limit, the thing slips forward, the spring relaxes and the thing sticks again. This repeats many times a second or just once in a while. It is called stick-slip.
examples: A chalk squeaks on a blackboard because it sticks and slips again and again.
A violin or sarangi bow makes a string vibrate by sticking to the string and slipping off it, thousands of times each second.
A rusty door hinge squeaks for the same reason.
explanations.art: A graph drawn as saw teeth, with a box and a spring beside it, showing the force going up and dropping again and again.
explanations.context: This card explains the jerks that you see when you do the Walking Ruler activity.

explanations.definition: Rolling friction is the friction on a wheel or ball that rolls instead of sliding. It is usually much smaller than sliding friction.
explanations.description: A wheel does not slide along the ground. It rolls. The patch of the wheel that touches the ground is for a moment still, so it does not rub. Because of this, rolling friction is usually many times smaller than sliding friction. This is why a wheeled suitcase is easy to pull and a dragged one is hard. A ball bearing puts rolling balls between two parts that turn, so even the axle can roll instead of slide. Rolling friction is not zero. Wheels and the road squash a little as they roll, and this takes energy.
examples: Pencils laid under a heavy book let you push the book with one finger.
Ball bearings sit inside bicycle hubs, ceiling fans and skateboard wheels.
A railway wheel on a steel rail has very low rolling friction, so a train can pull a very heavy load.
explanations.art: A heavy book on three pencils with a small arrow, next to the same book dragged with a long arrow.
explanations.context: This card explains the Rollers and Marbles activity.

explanations.definition: Fluid friction is the friction inside a liquid or gas and on things that move through it. Viscosity is how large it is.
explanations.description: A liquid has friction too. Its layers rub against each other, and against anything that moves through it. This is called fluid friction. How strong it is depends on the liquid. The word for how thick and slow a liquid is, is viscosity. Honey is thousands of times more viscous than water. A ball falls through honey slowly and through water quickly. Warm honey flows more easily than cold honey, because heat makes the molecules move faster and slip past each other more easily. Engine oil is made to thin out in a controlled way as the engine warms, so it keeps working from a cold morning to a hot road.
examples: Honey, ghee and coconut oil all flow faster after they are warmed.
A boat feels the friction of water as it moves, and a cyclist feels the friction of air.
Engine oil and the oil in a bicycle chain keep metal parts from rubbing directly.
explanations.art: A marble falling in a tall glass of water and in a tall glass of honey, with arrows of different length for the speed.
explanations.context: This card explains the Slow Drop activity.

explanations.concept: The rope rule: why turns multiply the grip
explanations.definition: When a rope is wound round a post, each extra turn multiplies the load that a light pull can hold by the same number.
explanations.description: A rope wound round a post holds a heavy load with a light pull. Every part of the rope that touches the post adds a little friction. The more rope touches the post, the more friction there is. Here is the surprising part. Each extra turn does not add the same amount. It multiplies the grip by the same number. If the first turn makes the hold six times easier, the second turn makes it six times easier again, so two turns make it thirty-six times easier. The number depends on the rope and the post. Leonhard Euler worked out this rule in the 1700s. Sailors and boatmen had been using it for thousands of years before anyone wrote it down.
examples: A boat is held on a bollard with three or four turns of rope and a light hold on the tail.
A knot in a shoelace holds because each crossing of the lace is a turn with friction.
Rock climbers wind a rope through a device so that a light hold can catch a fall.
explanations.art: A rope wound once, twice and three times round a post with a smaller and smaller hand on the end.
explanations.context: This card explains the Wrap the Thread test and the story.

explanations.description: Living beings are experts in friction. A gecko's toes carry millions of tiny hairs. Each hair is split into even tinier ends that get so close to a surface that the pull between atoms holds them on. A tree frog has toe pads that are wet and patterned, and they grip wet leaves. Your own fingertips have ridges called fingerprints. Skin with a little moisture grips best. Scientists still disagree about why fingers wrinkle in water. Some think the wrinkles are channels that help grip wet things, like the tread on a tyre. Other experiments found little or no help.
examples: A gecko can walk across a glass ceiling.
A tree frog's toes grip a wet leaf in the rain.
A mountain climber's chalk dries the hands, and a surgeon's glove keeps a grip.

perspectives.explanation: Wet fingers wrinkle into channels, like the tread of a tyre, so that water can drain away and the fingers grip better in the rain.

perspectives.who: Kyriacos Kareklas, Daniel Nettle and Tom Smulders, 2013
perspectives.explanation: In a test, people with wrinkled fingers picked up wet objects faster than people with smooth fingers. They found no difference with dry objects.

perspectives.who: Other researchers who repeated the test
perspectives.explanation: Some other experiments found no clear help from wrinkles, so scientists are still arguing about it.

explanations.art: A gecko's foot with a zoomed picture of the hairs on a toe, and beside it a fingertip with ridges.
explanations.context: This card is about how animals, including us, grip. Scientists do not agree about everything here.

explanations.definition: The work done against friction is the friction force times the distance moved. It ends up as heat.
explanations.description: To drag a box across a floor, you must keep pushing, and you do work. Scientists measure the work as the pushing force times the distance. This work does not disappear. It turns into heat, as the surfaces and the air warm up a little. If the friction force is 5 newtons and you drag the box 10 metres, you do 5 times 10, which is 50 joules of work, and all 50 joules end up as heat. Wheels and oil lower the friction force, so the same journey costs less energy. All over the world, a large share of the fuel used by machines goes into overcoming friction.
examples: A cyclist's legs do work against friction in the chain, the tyres and the air.
Brake pads get hot, because the movement of the vehicle turns into heat in the brakes.
Rubbing your hands warms them, because your push does work against friction.
explanations.art: A box being dragged 10 metres, with a number 5 on the pull arrow, a number 10 on the distance and a red heat glow at the bottom of the box.
explanations.context: This card links friction to energy, which is the idea behind the question: where does the movement go?

agreed.text: On a flat, dry surface, friction is roughly proportional to how hard the two surfaces press together.
agreed.evidence: People have pulled loaded blocks along tables with spring scales since the 1600s. The pull needed grows close to evenly with the load for hard, dry surfaces.

agreed.text: On hard, dry surfaces, friction hardly changes with the size of the face that touches.
agreed.evidence: Amontons found this in 1699 and Coulomb confirmed it in 1785. It is easy to test with a brick on its big face and its narrow end.

agreed.text: Two surfaces touch only at the tips of their bumps, a tiny part of the area you can see.
agreed.evidence: Bowden and Tabor measured how well electricity passed between pressed metal surfaces. It passed through only tiny spots.

agreed.text: Rolling friction is usually much smaller than sliding friction.
agreed.evidence: Loads can be moved on rollers or wheels with a fraction of the force needed to drag them. Engineers have measured the difference for centuries.

agreed.text: The work done against friction turns into heat.
agreed.evidence: Rumford (1798) and Joule (1840s) showed that rubbing and stirring make heat in exact amounts.

challenging.claim: Two flat things pressed together touch each other all over.
challenging.who: Almost everyone, because the surfaces look and feel smooth.
challenging.for: A mirror, a glass tumbler and a polished tile look perfectly flat and smooth.
challenging.against: Under a microscope, every surface is full of peaks. Electricity passes between two pressed metal plates through only tiny spots. The real touching area is much smaller than it looks.

challenging.claim: A bigger face always has more friction than a smaller face.
challenging.for: More of the box is touching the floor, so it seems it should grip more.
challenging.against: For hard, dry things, the same weight spreads over more bumps, each pressed less. The total grip is nearly the same. Soft rubber and sticky tape are exceptions.

challenging.claim: Friction is a fixed number that is always at its maximum.
challenging.for: Friction always seems to be 'in the way'.
challenging.against: When you push a heavy cupboard gently and it does not move, friction pushes back exactly as hard as you push. It rises as you push, up to a limit. After the limit, the cupboard moves.

challenging.claim: To hold a heavy boat, you need a strong pull.
challenging.who: Anyone who has not used a rope round a post.
challenging.for: The boat is heavy, so it feels as if it needs a big force to hold it.
challenging.against: A rope round a post multiplies the grip with every turn. A child can hold a boat with a light pull after a few turns.

challenging.claim: Wrinkled fingers are made to give a better grip in the rain.
challenging.who: Mark Changizi, a scientist, and others, from 2011.
challenging.for: The wrinkles look like tyre tread, and one experiment found that wrinkled fingers pick up wet things faster.
challenging.against: Some other experiments found no clear help. Scientists do not agree.

big_questions.q: Doubling the load doubles the grip. If the surface looks the same, what must have changed underneath?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tiny peaks on both surfaces, and what happens to them when you press harder.

big_questions.q: A wide face and a narrow face grip about the same. Is the grip in how much of the box you can see?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the weight is doing when it is spread out or squeezed in.

big_questions.q: If two surfaces really touch only at a few tiny spots, are they touching at all in the places between?
big_questions.hint: Think about how close is close enough to count as touching.

big_questions.q: Each turn of a rope makes the grip several times stronger. Why does adding one more turn help more and more?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens when each turn multiplies the one before.

big_questions.q: Rolling has much less friction than sliding. What does a wheel do that a sliding box cannot?
big_questions.hint: Think about the spot where the wheel touches the ground.

big_questions.q: Stick-slip makes a violin sing and also makes an earthquake. Is it the same thing?
big_questions.hint: Think about what sticks, what slips and how big each one is.

big_questions.q: Boatmen used the rope rule long before Euler wrote it down. Who really knew it first?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between being able to do something and being able to say why it works.

big_questions.q: Honey makes a ball fall slowly, and water lets it fall fast. Is a slow fall a kind of grip?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the liquid is doing to the ball as it falls.

big_questions.q: Where does touching end and being joined begin? Is a sticker touching a wall or part of it?
big_questions.hint: Think about two atoms close to each other, and what pulls them together.

story.title: The Fourth Turn
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. A rope wound round a post holds a heavy load with a light pull, and each extra turn makes the hold several times stronger. The boat, the quay and the people are imagined.
text: On the evening the rain came early, Anjana sat on the warm steps of the old quay at Fort Kochi with a bobbin of cotton thread in her lap. She was ten, and she had a problem. That morning her teacher had asked the class a question. How many turns of thread round a pencil would hold up a bottle of water? Anjana had tried one turn, and the bottle slid down and bumped her toes. She had tried two turns, and it slid again, only more slowly.

Her grandmother, Kalyani Ammamma, sat beside her, shelling tamarind pods. Ammamma was seventy-three. When she was young, she and her husband had run a cargo boat up and down the backwaters, and her hands were as brown and tough as old rope. 'Your thread is slippery,' she said, without looking up. 'So you must ask it for more.' 'More what?' asked Anjana. Ammamma only smiled and went on shelling.

Anjana wound the thread round the pencil again. This time she did not stop at two turns. She went on to three. She hung the little bottle from one end and held the other end between two fingers, hardly pinching at all. The bottle did not fall. Anjana stared at it. Three turns held it. Two turns had not. She did not understand how one more turn could change so much.

Then the sky turned the colour of wet slate, and the wind came across the water in a long, cold push. Out in the harbour, a big cargo boat called the Lakshmi was coming in, loaded to the rim with coconuts. She was meant to stop at the iron post at the end of the quay. But the wind was behind her, and she kept coming, faster than the boatman had planned.

A rope flew from the deck. Rashid, who worked on the quay, caught it. Thomas, the young man beside him, grabbed the rope behind him. They leaned back with their heels in the wet stone and pulled with all their weight. The boat did not slow. The rope hissed through their hands. 'Let go!' shouted Rashid. 'It's burning!' They let go. The rope skittered across the stones, and the Lakshmi began to swing towards the stone arch of the old bridge.

Ammamma stood up. She did not run. She walked to the iron post, picked up the rope as it slid by, and made one loop round the post. Then a second. Then a third. She held the loose end in her right hand, as lightly as if she were holding a flower. The rope groaned against the iron. Anjana watched her grandmother's hand. It was hardly pulling at all. But the rope did not run free. It slid, slowly, a hand's width at a time, and every hand's width it slid, the boat slowed down.

'It is still too fast,' Anjana whispered. The boat was huge, and the post was shuddering. The rope began to slide faster, and the loose end tugged hard in her grandmother's hand. Anjana jumped to her feet. She thought of her bottle. One turn had slid. Two had slid, more slowly. Three had held. Each turn had made the holding easier, not by a little, but by a lot. 'Ammamma!' she shouted. 'One more turn!'

Ammamma did not ask why. She slipped a fourth loop round the post. The rope bit. The loose end went quiet in her hand. The Lakshmi slid on for the length of two bullock carts, slower and slower, and then she stopped with a soft bump, one arm's length from the arch of the bridge. Coconuts rolled in the hold, and then everything was still. The first fat drops of rain began to fall on the stones.

Rashid and Thomas stood with their palms open. They were red as chillies. 'How?' said Rashid. 'Two of us could not hold her, and you did it with one hand.' Ammamma shook out her fingers. 'I did not hold the boat,' she said. 'The post held the boat. I only held the tail of the rope, and the turns did the rest.' She looked at Anjana. 'My hands knew three turns. She knew why a fourth would work.'

Rashid shook his head, but he was smiling. 'Show me,' he said. Ammamma took his wrist. 'Never pull,' she said. 'Wind the rope, and then ease. Too few turns, and the rope runs. Too many, and the boat stops with a jerk and breaks the line. A little slip is a friend.' Thomas knelt and put his hand on the wet iron post. It was warm.

That night, Anjana wound her thread round the pencil again. Four turns. She hung the bottle from one end, and she held the other end with just one finger. The bottle hung in the lamplight, perfectly still. She did not need the lesson to be any bigger than that. The thread was holding a bottle, and the pencil was holding the thread, and neither was doing very much at all.
story.epiphany: A rope wound round a post holds a heavy boat with a light pull, because every turn multiplies the grip by the same number. One more turn can make the hold several times easier.
ask: Why did the fourth turn help more than a fourth person pulling would have?
Why did Ammamma let the rope slip a little, instead of locking it with many turns right away?
What would have happened if the post had been wet with oil?
